terms.definition: A whirling region of gas or fluid weather — on Jupiter, the Great Red Spot is the biggest known one.
terms.function: Explains why the Great Red Spot is moving, churning weather, not a solid mark.
terms.whereItIs: The recessed oval on Jupiter's face in the model.
terms.whyItMatters: Jupiter's storm is wide enough to swallow Earth, and has persisted for at least 190 years — weather on a scale Earth can't produce.

terms.definition: A broad, gently sloping volcano built up by layer after layer of lava flows — Olympus Mons is the tallest known.
terms.function: Explains Olympus Mons's wide, low profile and how it grew to 22 km tall without plate tectonics moving its hotspot.
terms.whereItIs: The low dome with a caldera ring on Mars's face.
terms.whyItMatters: Olympus Mons is nearly three times Mount Everest's height — the biggest volcanic mountain known anywhere.

terms.definition: A canyon formed when the ground pulls apart along cracks — Valles Marineris is the solar system's grandest example.
terms.function: Explains Valles Marineris's straight, branched shape and its record length of over 4,000 km.
terms.whereItIs: The shallow V-groove wrapping partway around Mars's equator in the model.
terms.whyItMatters: It would stretch across the entire United States — and it records Mars's tectonic and watery history.

terms.definition: A flat disc of countless separate particles orbiting a planet — each chunk its own tiny moon.
terms.function: Explains how the 'sheets' of Saturn's rings can stay up: every ice chunk is in its own orbit.
terms.whereItIs: The pale gold torus around Saturn in the model.
terms.whyItMatters: Rings are not solid — they are trillions of ice-and-rock bodies, from dust grains to house-sized boulders.

terms.definition: The dark patches on the Moon — ancient plains of solidified lava that flooded giant impact basins.
terms.function: Explains the Moon's dark 'seas' — volcanic rock, not water.
terms.whereItIs: The three dark oval patches on the Moon sphere in the model.
terms.whyItMatters: The maria record the massive impacts and volcanism of the young solar system — and their name comes from early astronomers who really thought they were seas.
